days.title: HCP Terraform: Workspaces And Remote Runs

days.title: Capstone: Prove It And Write It Up

tasks.title: Destroy the whole environment and rebuild it from code alone. Time it.
List every manual step you needed, fix each one in code, then rebuild again.
Have a friend break one thing anywhere in the stack without telling you what.
Diagnose and fix it using your dashboards, logs and checklists. Record how long it took.
Write the project up: architecture, decisions, pipeline, observability and measured outcomes.
Push everything and pin the repository. This is the project you will be interviewed on.

questions.prompt: What is a workspace in HCP Terraform?
options: A managed unit holding state, variables and run history for one environment
questions.explanation: Each workspace owns its own state and configuration inputs, and runs execute against it.

questions.prompt: What is a speculative plan?
options: A plan run for review, typically on a pull request, that never applies
questions.explanation: It shows the effect of a proposed change without changing anything.

questions.prompt: What does connecting a workspace to a version control repository achieve?
options: Changes in the repository trigger runs automatically
questions.explanation: The repository becomes the source of truth and pushes drive the workflow.

questions.prompt: What is a variable set used for?
options: Sharing the same variables across multiple workspaces
questions.explanation: It avoids defining the same values separately in every workspace.

questions.prompt: What does Sentinel do?
options: Enforces policy rules against a plan before it can be applied
questions.explanation: It sits between plan and apply so non compliant changes are stopped.

questions.prompt: What is the private module registry for?
options: Publishing and versioning modules within your own organisation
questions.explanation: Teams reuse internal modules with proper versioning rather than copying code.

questions.prompt: Where does Terraform install provider plugins?
options: In a local directory during init
questions.explanation: Init downloads and caches the providers the configuration requires.

questions.prompt: Which command would you use to see the current value of an output?
questions.explanation: The output command prints declared outputs from the current state.

questions.prompt: Which of these is outside the core write, plan, apply workflow?
questions.explanation: Import, state commands and console are tools you reach for in specific situations.

questions.prompt: Why does the documentation describe provisioners as a last resort?
options: They break the declarative model and are hard to make reliable
questions.explanation: They run imperative steps that Terraform cannot reason about or reconcile.

questions.prompt: What does terraform console let you do?
options: Evaluate expressions against the current state
questions.explanation: It is the fastest way to check a function or interpolation before using it.

questions.prompt: What is one advantage of HCP Terraform over an S3 backend with DynamoDB?
options: Remote execution, run history and policy enforcement in one place
questions.explanation: The managed service adds workflow features on top of state storage and locking.

questions.prompt: Terraform is described as cloud agnostic because provider plugins let it manage many platforms.
questions.explanation: The core is the same regardless of target, and the provider handles the specific API.

questions.prompt: A speculative plan can change infrastructure if the plan succeeds.
questions.explanation: It exists specifically to show the effect without applying anything.

questions.prompt: Knowing which HCP Terraform features are paid is worth revising because the exam asks about it.
questions.explanation: Tier awareness appears in the objectives even though it rarely matters day to day.

questions.prompt: What is the most effective final stage of exam preparation?
options: Timed practice exams with full review of every wrong answer
Rereading the documentation cover to cover
questions.explanation: Practice under time reveals both knowledge gaps and reading speed problems.

questions.prompt: Why record practice scores by objective?
options: So you revise the weak areas instead of spreading effort evenly
questions.explanation: Even revision wastes the limited time you have on things you already know.

questions.prompt: You are at sixty five percent a few days before the date. What is the sensible action?
options: Move the date and close the gaps
questions.explanation: Moving a date costs less than a failed attempt in both money and confidence.

questions.prompt: Why check the vendor page rather than a blog for exam details?
options: Exam versions and formats change and third party posts go stale
questions.explanation: Only the vendor page is guaranteed to describe the exam you will actually sit.

questions.prompt: Why explain a weak topic out loud before the exam?
options: Stumbling shows precisely where your understanding is thin
questions.explanation: Spoken explanation exposes gaps that silent reading hides.

questions.prompt: What should you do the evening before an exam?
questions.explanation: Tiredness costs more marks than the last hour of revision could gain.

questions.prompt: What does a certification actually prove?
options: That you can run production systems
That you know the concepts and vocabulary
That you can be hired without projects
questions.explanation: It gets you past filters, and your projects carry the interview.

questions.prompt: Why publish a new certification the same day you earn it?
options: Because recruiters search on it and momentum matters
questions.explanation: An unlisted credential does nothing for you.

questions.prompt: If you fail, when should you write the retake plan?
options: The same day, while you remember which areas hurt
Only if the score was close
questions.explanation: Your recall of the weak areas is most accurate immediately afterwards.

questions.prompt: Why is a certification stronger when paired with a public project?
options: The exam shows knowledge and the project shows application
questions.explanation: Together they answer both what you know and what you have actually done.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a one page cheat sheet in the final days?
options: To consolidate the facts that keep slipping
questions.explanation: The act of writing it is the revision, and it concentrates what will not stick.

questions.prompt: What should you do with a practice question you got right by guessing?
options: Review it as if you got it wrong
questions.explanation: A lucky guess is an unmarked gap that will reappear in the real exam.

questions.prompt: Two certifications backed by real projects is a stronger position than four certifications with none.
questions.explanation: Employers discount certificate stacking without evidence of application.

questions.prompt: Reviewing wrong answers matters more than repeating practice exams endlessly.
questions.explanation: The learning is in understanding the reasoning, not in accumulating attempt counts.

questions.prompt: Booking the exam only once you are consistently scoring above eighty percent is a reasonable rule.
questions.explanation: It converts a hopeful attempt into a likely pass, and the rule protects you from optimism.

questions.prompt: What question do metrics answer that logs do not?
options: Why did this specific request fail
How is the system behaving over time
questions.explanation: Metrics show trends and aggregates, while logs explain individual events.

questions.prompt: What are the four golden signals?
questions.explanation: They describe user visible health rather than machine internals.

questions.prompt: Why alert on symptoms rather than causes?
options: Because users experience symptoms, and causes vary
questions.explanation: High CPU may be fine, while slow responses are always a problem worth waking up for.

questions.prompt: Why is structured logging better than plain text lines?
options: You can query by field instead of matching text patterns
questions.explanation: Fields make filtering and aggregation reliable instead of fragile.

questions.prompt: What does a request identifier in every log line give you?
options: The ability to follow one request across components
questions.explanation: Correlation is what turns scattered lines into a single story.

questions.prompt: Why is debug level logging expensive in production?
options: Volume drives storage and query costs, and hides the important lines
questions.explanation: Both the bill and the signal to noise ratio suffer.

questions.prompt: How should you choose an alert threshold?
options: Base it on your own observed baseline
questions.explanation: A threshold that does not reflect your normal behaviour produces noise or silence.

questions.prompt: What should be attached to every alert?
options: A short runbook saying what to check first
questions.explanation: The person woken at 3am needs a starting point, not a puzzle.

questions.prompt: What should you do with an alert you would not act on?
questions.explanation: Alerts nobody acts on train people to ignore all alerts, including the real ones.

questions.prompt: What does distributed tracing add beyond logs and metrics?
options: The path and timing of one request across multiple services
questions.explanation: It shows where the time went when several components are involved.

questions.prompt: Why define dashboards and alarms in Terraform?
options: So monitoring is versioned and rebuilt with the environment
questions.explanation: Monitoring created by hand disappears the next time the environment is rebuilt.

questions.prompt: What is a service level objective?
options: A stated target for a measurable aspect of service quality
questions.explanation: It defines what good looks like in numbers, which is what alerts should protect.

questions.prompt: Learning about an outage from your alert rather than by checking manually is the goal.
questions.explanation: If you find problems by looking, your monitoring is not doing its job.

questions.prompt: You should test that an alert fires by deliberately causing the condition.
questions.explanation: An untested alert is an assumption, and it usually fails on the day it matters.

questions.prompt: Monitoring answers known questions, while observability helps investigate problems you did not anticipate.
questions.explanation: The distinction matters because you cannot build a dashboard for a failure you have never seen.

questions.prompt: Where should projects sit on your CV given your background?
questions.explanation: Projects are your strongest evidence, so they should be read first.

questions.prompt: Which CV bullet is strongest?
options: Cut deployment time from 20 minutes to under 2 by automating the release pipeline
questions.explanation: An outcome with a number shows what changed because you were there.

questions.prompt: Why tailor a second CV for cloud support roles?
options: Because different roles emphasise different evidence from the same work
questions.explanation: The same projects can be framed toward troubleshooting or toward building.

questions.prompt: What should a project README contain?
options: A diagram, what it does, how to run it, and what you learned
questions.explanation: A reviewer decides in under a minute, and the README is what they read.

questions.prompt: Why clone your own repository to a clean machine and follow your README?
options: Because the instructions almost always assume something only your machine has
questions.explanation: It is the same lesson as the works on my machine problem, applied to documentation.

questions.prompt: What should a LinkedIn headline say?
options: What you build and the roles you are targeting
questions.explanation: Recruiters search for what you do, not for what you are currently learning.

questions.prompt: Why read twenty real job postings before applying?
options: To find the most common requirements you do not yet meet
questions.explanation: The postings tell you what the gap actually is, rather than what you assume it is.

questions.prompt: Why send a message to a person rather than only applying through job boards?
options: Applications from a real conversation get read far more often
questions.explanation: A named contact moves you out of a pile of hundreds.

questions.prompt: How should you answer a walk me through your diagnosis question?
options: Describe your checks in order, from your machine outwards
questions.explanation: Interviewers are testing your method, not whether you guess the cause.

questions.prompt: What makes a good failure story in an interview?
options: A failure that was someone else's fault
An honest mistake and the specific change you made afterwards
questions.explanation: The change you made is the part they are actually assessing.

questions.prompt: Why record yourself answering a technical question?
options: To hear the filler and the parts where you lose the thread
questions.explanation: You cannot hear your own hesitation while you are speaking.

questions.prompt: Why prepare questions to ask the interviewer?
options: Because what you ask shows how you think about running systems
questions.explanation: Good questions about on call, deployment and incidents signal real understanding.

questions.prompt: Preparing job materials in April rather than the final week is a deliberate protection against running out of time.
questions.explanation: The job hunt work is always what gets squeezed, so it is moved earlier on purpose.

questions.prompt: A CV listing tools without outcomes is weaker than one listing fewer tools with measured results.
questions.explanation: Anyone can list tools, and outcomes are what distinguish candidates.

questions.prompt: Having someone unfamiliar with your work read your CV is a useful test of whether it communicates.
questions.explanation: If they cannot say what you do after one read, the CV has failed its main job.

questions.prompt: What should you do before building the capstone?
options: Define requirements, draw the architecture and estimate the cost
questions.explanation: Design decisions are far cheaper to change on paper than in a running environment.

questions.prompt: Why write down the alternatives you rejected?
options: Because interviewers ask why you chose one approach over another
questions.explanation: Explaining a trade off is what separates a builder from someone following a tutorial.

questions.prompt: Why keep the capstone small?
options: Because a finished small project beats an abandoned large one
questions.explanation: Scope is the most common reason a portfolio project never gets finished.

questions.prompt: How should staging and production differ in the capstone?
options: Same code and modules, different variable values and sizes
questions.explanation: Reusing the code with different inputs is what makes promotion trustworthy.

questions.prompt: What does a rollback test prove?
options: That you can recover from a bad release quickly
questions.explanation: Deploying is easy, and recovering is what actually matters under pressure.

questions.prompt: Why deploy a deliberately broken build during the capstone?
options: To prove the rollback path works before you need it
questions.explanation: An untested rollback is a plan, not a capability.

questions.prompt: Why define alarms and dashboards in Terraform for the capstone?
options: So they are rebuilt automatically with the environment
questions.explanation: Monitoring built by hand disappears on the next rebuild and is never noticed until an incident.

questions.prompt: What does the destroy and rebuild exercise reveal?
options: Every manual step still hidden in your process
questions.explanation: Anything you had to click is a gap, and this is the only reliable way to find them.

questions.prompt: After finding manual steps, what is the correct next action?
options: Fix each in code and rebuild again to confirm
questions.explanation: The second clean rebuild is the proof, and documentation alone makes them permanent.

questions.prompt: Why time your diagnosis during the sabotage exercise?
options: Because time to recovery is a real operational metric you can quote
questions.explanation: A measured recovery time is far more convincing than saying you fixed it.

questions.prompt: What belongs in the capstone write up?
options: Architecture, decisions, pipeline, observability and measured outcomes
questions.explanation: Those five sections answer every question an interviewer is likely to ask.

questions.prompt: Why is this the project you will be interviewed on?
options: It is the only one covering design, automation, deployment and operations together
questions.explanation: It demonstrates the whole loop, which no single earlier project does on its own.

questions.prompt: Estimating monthly cost before building is part of designing responsibly.
questions.explanation: Architecture drives the bill, so the estimate belongs at design time, not after the invoice.

questions.prompt: A capstone with no monitoring can still demonstrate that you can operate a system.
questions.explanation: Operating means knowing when something breaks, and without monitoring you would find out from a user.

questions.prompt: Following your own README on a clean machine is a fair test of whether the project is genuinely reproducible.
questions.explanation: If you cannot reproduce it from your own instructions, nobody else can either.
